## The one-paragraph version {.unnumbered}

Every guide-assignment method answers the same question for each (guide $g$, cell $c$): **is the
observed count $N_{g,c}$ larger than ambient contamination alone would produce?** Answering it
requires an estimate of the ambient-noise level, and that estimate must be built from the count
matrix itself — which contains the very signal we are trying to detect. **Signal leaks into the
estimate of its own null.** Laid out on a $2\times2$ contingency table, the leak lands in exactly
three cells, and each published method is characterized by *which of those cells it cleans*.
Cleaning the two "other-cell" cells removes a Simpson's-paradox **false-positive** inflation
(fishash); cleaning the third, the focal cell's own-signal cell, removes a **power loss** that masks
co-occurring guides at high MOI (CLEANSER, in effect). No prior method cleans all three; ours does,
using an estimate fishash already computes and discards.

---

## The estimand: one test, repeated {#sec-estimand}

Write the observed guide-count matrix as a sum of two latent parts,
$$
N_{g,c} \;=\; S_{g,c} \;+\; Z_{g,c},
$$
where $S_{g,c}$ counts UMIs from guide molecules **truly integrated** in cell $c$ (*signal*) and
$Z_{g,c}$ counts UMIs from **ambient contamination** — soup, chimeras, index hopping (*noise*).
Assignment is the family of hypotheses
$$
H_0^{(g,c)}: S_{g,c} = 0 \quad\text{(guide $g$ was never in cell $c$)}
\qquad\text{vs}\qquad
H_1^{(g,c)}: S_{g,c} > 0 .
$$
Under $H_0$, $N_{g,c}=Z_{g,c}$ is *pure noise*, so a test reduces to: **is $N_{g,c}$ surprisingly
large for noise?** Everything below is a way of pinning down "for noise."

## The noise model is rank-1 {#sec-rank1}

Ambient contamination has a natural low-rank form. A contaminating UMI lands in cell $c$ in
proportion to how much soup $c$ absorbed and how deep it was sequenced — a **cell exposure**
$d_c$ — and it reads as guide $g$ in proportion to $g$'s share of the ambient pool — a **guide
abundance** $a_g$. If those are independent in the noise (fishash's Prop-1 assumption), then
$$
\mathbb{E}[Z_{g,c}] \;=\; a_g\, d_c ,
$$
a rank-1 outer product. This is not a modeling flourish; it is the same object three different ways:

- It is the **independence / two-way log-linear model** $\log \mathbb{E}[Z_{g,c}] = \alpha_g +
  \beta_c$, whose Poisson MLE fitted values are exactly the contingency-table expected counts
  $N_{g,:}N_{:,c}/N_{:,:}$.
- It is therefore the null of **Fisher's exact / hypergeometric test** on the $2\times2$ table —
  conditioning on the margins tests departure *above the rank-1 fit*.
- It is, verbatim, what **fishash estimates** when it fits
  $\hat Z_{g,c} = \gamma_g\kappa_c$ by rank-1 Poisson completion (its Eq 8–9).

So "test $N_{g,c}$ against its margins" and "test against a fitted rank-1 ambient model" are the
same statement. The methods differ only in **how they fit that model in the presence of signal.**

## The one hard problem: a test statistic contaminated by its own alternative {#sec-problem}

To test $H_0^{(g,c)}$ we need the noise rate $a_g d_c$, estimated from the matrix. But the matrix is
$S+Z$. Look at the $2\times2$ table for $(g,c)$ (fishash Eq 1–2), written in the $S+Z$ decomposition:

|                    | cell $c$                          | other cells $-c$                       |
|--------------------|-----------------------------------|----------------------------------------|
| **guide $g$**      | $N_{g,c}=Z_{g,c}$ *(pure noise under $H_0$)* | $N_{g,-c}=Z_{g,-c}+\,S_{g,-c}$ |
| **other guides**   | $N_{-g,c}=Z_{-g,c}+\,S_{-g,c}$    | $N_{-g,-c}=Z_{-g,-c}+\,S_{-g,-c}$      |

with empirical odds ratio $\hat R_{g,c} = \dfrac{N_{g,c}\,N_{-g,-c}}{N_{-g,c}\,N_{g,-c}}$ and a
one-sided test of $H_0:R_{g,c}\le 1$.

Under $H_0$ the cell we are testing, $N_{g,c}$, is clean noise. **Signal contaminates the other
three cells** — and each contaminated cell pushes the test statistic a definite way:

| Background cell | What signal leaks in | Position in $\hat R$ | Effect of the leak |
|---|---|:--:|---|
| $N_{-g,-c}$ | other guides' signal in other cells (**large**) | numerator | inflates $\hat R$ → **false positive** |
| $N_{g,-c}$ | guide $g$'s signal in the cells that truly carry it | denominator | deflates $\hat R$ → conservative for $g$ |
| $N_{-g,c}$ | **cell $c$'s own** true guide(s) | denominator | deflates $\hat R$ → conservative for co-occurring guides |

Two of these are the failure modes that separate the methods.

## Two failure modes {#sec-failuremodes}

### Failure mode A — Simpson's paradox → false positives (calibration) {#sec-simpson}

The dominant leak is into $N_{-g,-c}$. Whatever guides are abundant as signal deposit their large
counts into this "everything else, elsewhere" cell, inflating the numerator of $\hat R$ and making a
**mere-noise** count $N_{g,c}$ look enriched. fishash's Prop 1 makes this exact: even with $g$ truly
absent from $c$ and $g,c$ noise-independent, $\hat R_{g,c}>1$ can hold — a false positive with **no
signal in the tested cell at all**.

The paper's cartoon (Fig 2a) is the cleanest illustration. In cell $c$: $g$ has 1 (noise), other
guides have 2 → ratio $1/2=0.5$. In other cells: $g$ has $9$ ($1$ signal $+8$ noise), other guides
have $31$ ($23$ signal $+8$ noise) → ratio $9/31\approx0.29$. So
$\hat R = 0.5/0.29 \approx 1.7 > 1$ — spurious enrichment. The culprit is the $23$ signal reads of
*other* guides inflating the background denominator. Recompute the background on **noise only**:
$8/8=1.0$, giving $\hat R^\star = 0.5/1.0 = 0.5<1$ — corrected. This is anti-conservative and bites
whenever the background carries signal (dense / low-SNR regimes) → it is a **precision / FDR**
problem.

### Failure mode B — self-masking → power loss (high MOI) {#sec-depth}

The leak into $N_{-g,c}$ is different in character. This cell counts *other guides in the focal
cell* — and it is dominated by cell $c$'s **own** true guide(s). It sits in the denominator, so it
**deflates** $\hat R$: a strongly-transduced cell makes every *other* guide in it look like noise.
At low MOI this is harmless (there are no other real guides to miss), but **at high MOI a cell
carries several real guides that mutually mask each other** — the big primary guide inflates
$N_{-g,c}$ for the secondary guide, burying it. Equivalently, in the hypergeometric the focal cell's
exposure (the "draws" $N_{:,c}$) is overstated by its own signal, so the expected ambient count is
too high and true secondary guides fail to clear it. This is conservative → a **power / recall**
problem, and it is exactly the regime where fishash is documented to weaken.

**The two corrections are not redundant and not mirror images.** A cleans the *other-cells* column
to fix false positives; B cleans the *focal cell's own-signal* to fix false negatives. Different
cells, opposite directions, different regimes.

## The cleaning tool, and who uses it {#sec-tool}

All the "cleaning" needs the same object: an estimate of the **noise-only** counts $\hat Z$. fishash
supplies it by fitting the rank-1 model to the matrix with the currently-assigned (signal) entries
**masked** — $\hat Z_{g,c}=\gamma_g\kappa_c$ maximizing the masked Poisson likelihood, iterated so
that as more signal is assigned and masked, the fit sharpens (Alg 1, Eq 8–9). This is precisely
robust estimation of the rank-1 null with its own alternative held out.

The decisive observation: **this single fit gives both a denoised guide abundance $\gamma_g$ and a
denoised cell exposure $\kappa_c$.** fishash uses $\hat Z$ to clean the two *other-cells* cells
(failure mode A) but plugs the **raw** $N_{:,c}$ back in for the focal cell's exposure — so it leaves
failure mode B in place. The correction for B is not new machinery; it is *using the $\kappa_c$
fishash already computed and threw away.*

This is one line in our reference implementation (`scripts/contingency_method.R`), which is written
precisely to ablate the two:

```r
# guide margin: denoised in BOTH modes (this IS fishash's Simpson correction, failure mode A)
K <- nr[i] - bgc + y
if (cell_margin == "ambient") {          # depth_fix (OURS): also fix failure mode B
  draws <- nc[j] - bgc + y               #   focal-cell exposure = DENOISED (kappa_c)
  pop   <- Tn - bgc + y
} else {                                 # cell_margin == "observed"  ==  fishash exactly
  draws <- obs_col[j]                    #   focal-cell exposure = RAW library size N_{:,c}
  pop   <- Tn - nc[j] + obs_col[j]
}
logp <- phyper(y - 1, K, pop - K, draws, lower.tail = FALSE, log.p = TRUE)
```

With `cell_margin="observed"` it reproduces fishash bit-for-bit; `"ambient"` swaps in the denoised
exposure. The whole contribution is which quantity supplies `draws`.

## Where the non-contingency methods sit {#sec-others}

Thresholds and per-guide mixtures attack the same estimand through a **one-dimensional, per-guide**
lens instead of the $2\times2$ table. That trade has a clean upside and a clean downside.

- **Naive threshold** ($N_{g,c}\ge t$): estimates neither $a_g$ nor $d_c$; assumes the noise level is
  a global constant. Exposed to *both* failure modes. Empirically the **"cutoff trap"**: fine on
  easy/low-ambient data, FDR blows up on high-ambient data (@sec-empirical).
- **Otsu / smoothed-valley:** per guide, split that guide's count distribution at the between-mode
  valley. This *does* separate $g$'s signal from $g$'s noise (a per-guide analogue of cleaning $a_g$),
  but uses **no cell information at all** — $d_c$ is not modeled, so it cannot tell a deep cell from a
  shallow one.
- **crispat (Poisson–Gauss):** per guide, a 2-component mixture (Poisson noise + Gaussian signal) on
  $\log_2$ non-zero counts. The latent component absorbs signal, so $g$'s noise rate is estimated
  cleanly — but again **no cell exposure term**. Borrows across cells, not across guides.
- **SCEPTRE (assignment mixture):** per guide, a latent-indicator Poisson GLM
  $\log\mu_j=\gamma X_j + o_j$ with a per-cell offset $o_j$ from covariates (including library size).
  The mixture cleans $g$'s rate (signal → the $X=1$ component) **and** it carries a cell exposure —
  but a **raw** covariate-based one, not a denoised ambient depth. *(Legacy quirk: the historical
  mixture adds the offset as $e^{o}+\gamma$ rather than $e^{o+\gamma}$; documented, works anyway.)*
- **CLEANSER:** a negative-binomial mixture with both a guide- and a **cell-specific normalization
  $L$**, where $L$ is built from the count of gRNAs with **$\le 2$ UMIs** in the cell — i.e. a
  deliberately **signal-free** estimate of the cell's ambient exposure. In our language, CLEANSER
  **cleans failure mode B** (via a hard low-count cutoff, inside a mixture) but has no Simpson
  correction for mode A.

The through-line: mixtures get a clean *guide* rate almost for free (the latent component eats the
signal), but they either ignore the cell exposure (crispat, Otsu) or use a raw one (SCEPTRE), and
they forgo the contingency table's borrowing of a **shared, denoisable** cell factor across guides.
CLEANSER is the exception that denoises the cell factor — the same insight as failure-mode-B, reached
in the mixture world.

## The map {#sec-map}

Two independent questions — is $g$'s noise rate estimated free of $g$'s signal? is $c$'s exposure
estimated free of $c$'s signal? — and the failure mode each leaves open:

| Method | Guide rate cleaned (mode A) | Cell exposure cleaned (mode B) | Exposed to |
|---|:--:|:--:|---|
| Fixed threshold | – | – | A **and** B |
| Otsu / valley | ✓ (per-guide split) | — (no cell term) | B (no depth) |
| crispat (Poisson–Gauss) | ✓ (mixture) | — (no cell term) | B (no depth) |
| SCEPTRE mixture | ✓ (mixture) | ✗ (raw offset) | B |
| geomux | ✗ (raw margins) | ✗ (raw) | A and B |
| our ambient test | ✗ (raw margins) | ✗ (raw) | A and B |
| **fishash** | **✓ (Simpson / masked rank-1)** | ✗ (raw $N_{:,c}$) | **B** |
| **CLEANSER** | ✗ (no Simpson) | **✓ ($L$ from $\le 2$)** | **A** |
| **depth_fix (ours)** | **✓** | **✓** | **—** |

fishash occupies "clean A only," CLEANSER "clean B only," in different frameworks. The empty
lower-right — clean both, in one test — is where our method sits, and it is a one-line reach from
fishash because fishash already computes the piece CLEANSER needs.

## Empirical fingerprints of the two failure modes {#sec-empirical}

The theory predicts specific, checkable signatures; the benchmarks show them. *(Sim figures are as
last recorded; the per-guide-fit sim redesign is edited but not re-run — treat as provisional.)*

- **Mode A is a precision effect.** In hard/low-SNR sim regimes, only methods **with** the Simpson
  correction reach precision $\ge 0.90$; the bare ambient test and geomux sit on a lower-precision
  frontier. The self-contained reproduction of fishash's Fig 7 nails the mechanism: uncorrected FDR
  $\approx0.20$ (fails nominal 5% in 10/10 reps) $\to$ corrected $\approx0.003$ (0/10), **recall
  unchanged**. Cleaning the other-cells column removes false positives without costing power — exactly
  a mode-A signature.
- **Mode B is a recall effect, MOI-graded.** Per-guide F1 at MOI 1/3/5: depth_fix
  **0.96 / 0.93 / 0.89** vs fishash 0.96 / 0.89 / 0.82. Identical at MOI 1 (no co-occurring guides to
  unmask), diverging as MOI rises (more mutual masking to undo) — exactly a mode-B signature, and
  exactly fishash's documented weak spot.
- **On real barnyard** (low-MOI, per-cell metric) depth_fix ties fishash (0.937 vs 0.942, no
  regression): with little mutual masking, fixing B costs nothing. The bare ambient test scores
  highest here (0.951) by being aggressive — i.e. by *lacking* the mode-A brake — which is the same
  coin as its low sim precision.
- **The cutoff trap** is the no-cleaning corner: a fixed $\ge 3$ threshold ties depth_fix on
  easy/low-ambient data but its FDR explodes to $\sim0.31$ on high-ambient (primary-cell) data where
  depth_fix holds $\sim0.027$.
- **CLEANSER**, once a scoring artifact is fixed (an un-thresholded posterior collapsing to "assign if
  count $\ge1$"), is competitive (Jaccard 0.893) — consistent with it having the mode-B fix.

## What is actually ours {#sec-ours}

Stated as narrowly as the reading supports:

1. The **cell exposure should be a denoised ambient depth, not raw library size** — but this is *not*
   our discovery. **CLEANSER got there first** (its $\le2$-count $L$). We credit it.
2. **fishash cleans the guide side, not the cell side** — verified from Eq 7 (draws $=N_{:,c}$) and
   from our own reproduction (`cell_margin="observed"` $\equiv$ fishash). So relative to fishash the
   denoised exposure is a real addition.
3. The contribution is **unification and economy:** decontaminate all three background cells of the
   $2\times2$ in a single hypergeometric test — fishash's mode-A correction *and* a denoised mode-B
   exposure — where the exposure is the $\kappa_c$ fishash's own rank-1 completion already produces
   and discards. It closes the empty corner of @sec-map and targets fishash's high-MOI weakness,
   beating it there while tying on real barnyard.

## Open questions {#sec-open}

- **Downstream arbiter.** All metrics here are upstream (assignment vs truth). The deciding test for
  FDR-vs-recall trade-offs is downstream **SCEPTRE DE** — negative-control calibration and power under
  each assignment. Not yet run.
- **depth_fix vs a correctly-scored CLEANSER**, head to head — the single most informative comparison
  for our claim, since CLEANSER shares the mode-B fix. Not yet done directly.
- **Estimator quality of the denoised exposure.** CLEANSER's hard $\le2$ cutoff vs our rank-1 noise
  column — which is the better ambient-depth estimator is untested.
- **Overdispersion (a possible failure mode C).** A conditional NB/beta-binomial tail rescues sim FDR
  under overdispersion but collapses on real barnyard (dispersion estimate not robust across
  chemistries). Keep the plain hypergeometric; revisit only if DE calibration demands it.
